nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the primary focus of the study discussed in the abstract?
nodes.answer: The study focuses on perceptions and conflicting worldviews of key actor groups in EU forest policy using Cultural Theory.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract This study employs Cultural Theory to study perceptions and conflicting worldviews of key actor groups in EU forest policy. Forests are central to different human demands for ecosystem services such as biomass, biodiversity, and climate mitigation. Tradeoffs occur between these ecosystem services, involving the necessity to set priorities. Related to increasing uncertainties inter alia caused by climate change, polarized perspectives prevail in the multi-level EU policy system regarding which evidence, whose attribution, and what optimal governance and management strategies are to be chosen for forests. At the core of these perspectives lie conflicting worldviews related to cultural biases of what is real and right. Through qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews with a diverse set of forest policy actors from the EU and member state level, the research delves into their percep- tions of EU forest policy, including perceived problems, preferred solutions, and assigned responsibilities, using a Cultural Theory lens. Our analysis distinguishes three groups of actors aligned with distinct elements of Cultural Theory worldviews while acknowledging the nuanced nature of these divisions. Our analysis invites readers to navigate the com- plexities of EU forest policy, unraveling worldviews and actor perspectives in pursuing informed policy decisions, and may eventually facilitate improved dialogue among actors considering these heterogeneous worldviews.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How has the coordination and integration of forest policy at the EU level been described?
nodes.answer: It has been described as weak.
nodes.paragraph: Consequently, a patchwork of EU forest-related policy instruments developed, each emphasizing its own priorities (e.g., renewable energy, nature protection, biodiversity conservation, and climate and land use policies) and preferred governance mechanism (such as state regulation, e.g. binding law, market-related governance, e.g. payment for ecosystem services, or community initiatives, e.g. awareness raising and capacity build- ing). This patchwork is prone to conflicts between policies, and forest policy coordina- tion and integration at the EU level has subsequently been described as weak (Aggestam & Giurca, 2021; P Izl et al., 2018; Wolfslehner et al., 2020). Addressing these challenges within the EU multi-level governance framework trig- gers polarized discussions. The increased issuance of policy instruments by the Euro- pean Commission, especially since the Green Deal, signals a growing interest in advancing EU forest policy (Aggestam & Giurca, 2021). Simultaneously, a political debate evolves around the legitimacy of the EU S legal competence on forests (Lazdinis et al., 2019; see also Onida, 2020), with some member states opposing EU competency as conflicting with their national interests (Wolfslehner et al., 2020).
